content: 1. Salicylate levels increase when administered at moderate doses but decrease at higher doses due to enhanced renal excretion of unchanged salicylic acid. 2. Teriparatide can increase calcium carbonate levels through pharmacodynamic synergy, but this interaction is considered minor. 3. Calcium carbonate and tetracycline interact by reducing each other's levels due to inhibition of gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. If co-administration is necessary, separate the doses by at least 2 hours and monitor the patient closely. 4. Calcium carbonate decreases the levels of tiludronate by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution, monitor closely, and separate administration by 30 minutes. 5. Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of timolol through an unspecified interaction mechanism and decreases its levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution, monitor closely, and separate administration by 2 hours. 6. Tobramycin decreases calcium carbonate levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. The significance of this interaction is unknown. 7. Torsemide decreases calcium carbonate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 8. Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of trandolapril through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Injectable triamcinolone acetonide suspension decreases calcium carbonate levels by increasing its elimination. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 10. Triamterene decreases calcium carbonate levels by increasing renal clearance. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 11. Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of ursodiol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 12. Calcium carbonate decreases the level or effect of vadadustat by binding to it in the gastrointestinal tract. Modify therapy as needed and monitor closely. Administer vadadustat at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after dosing with non-iron-containing phosphate binders. 13. Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of verapamil through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 14. Calcium carbonate decreases the level or effect of vismodegib due to an interaction that alters gastric pH, reducing vismodegib solubility and bioavailability. The effect on efficacy is unknown. Use caution and monitor closely. 15. The concurrent use of vitamin D with calcium salts is generally beneficial, but in some patients, this combination may lead to hypercalcemia. Monitor closely. 16. Calcium carbonate interacts with willow bark through passive renal tubular reabsorption due to increased pH. This interaction is minor, and its clinical significance is unknown. 17. Calcium carbonate decreases the levels of zoledronic acid by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution, monitor closely, and separate administration by 30 minutes. 18. Common adverse effects of calcium carbonate include anorexia, constipation, flatulence, nausea, vomiting, hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, milk-alkali syndrome, hypersensitivity, hypercalciuria, and renal calculi. 19. Long-term use of calcium carbonate may lead to hypercalcemia, which can exacerbate nephrolithiasis or cause generalized soft tissue and vascular calcification. It may also increase mortality in patients with chronic kidney disease. 20. Calcium carbonate absorption may be impaired in patients with achlorhydria, a condition common in the elderly. Consider using an alternative calcium salt form in such cases. 21. Hypercalciuria and hypercalcemia may occur in patients with hypoparathyroid disease who are receiving high doses of vitamin D. 22. Kidney stones have been reported with calcium carbonate use. Exercise caution in patients with a history of nephrolithiasis. 23. Use caution in patients with renal insufficiency, as they are more susceptible to the effects of excess calcium. 24. Advise patients to limit the intake of oxalate-rich foods (e.g., soy, green leafy vegetables, animal protein) to avoid reduced calcium absorption due to calcium-oxalate formation. 25. Calcium carbonate is classified as pregnancy category C. It is generally considered safe during lactation, as it crosses the placenta and appears in breast milk. 26. Calcium carbonate acts as an antacid by neutralizing gastric acidity. It is also used as a dietary supplement to prevent or treat negative calcium balance. Oral calcium supplements may protect against renal calculi formation by chelating with oxalate in the gut and preventing its absorption. 27. As a phosphate binder, calcium carbonate binds with dietary phosphate to form insoluble calcium phosphate, which is excreted in feces. 28. The bioavailability of calcium carbonate is approximately 25-35%, and food increases absorption by 10-30%. Its antacid action depends on gastric emptying time. 29. Peak plasma levels are reached within 20-60 minutes in the fasting state and up to 3 hours when ingested 1 hour after meals. Approximately 45% of calcium carbonate is protein-bound. 30. Renal clearance of calcium carbonate ranges from 50-300 mg/day. It is excreted primarily in feces as unabsorbed calcium (80%) and in urine (20%). 31. Calcium carbonate should be administered with food. Chewable tablets must be chewed or crushed completely before swallowing. 32. All formulations of calcium carbonate should be stored at 20-25°C (68-77°F) and should not be frozen.
